explanations.answer: He had been a foreigner in a foreign land
explanations.explanation: Moses had said, “I have been a foreigner in a foreign land.” (Exodus 18:3) That whole sentence got packed into one little boy's name. I think that's some serious packing, friend. I can barely get one word to fit on a cookie.

explanations.answer: He had been drawn out of the water
explanations.explanation: That water story belongs to Moses himself. Pharaoh's daughter, the Egyptian king's daughter, named him Moses because she drew him out of the water (Exodus 2:10). Gershom's reason is different. Moses had said, “I have been a foreigner in a foreign land.” (Exodus 18:3)

explanations.answer: He had found rest in a new home
explanations.explanation: The text gives Moses' own words, and they aren't about rest. He said, “I have been a foreigner in a foreign land.” (Exodus 18:3) I think that sounds like a man a long way from where he started. That's my guess, though. The text just gives us the words.

That's what the text says. Moses had said, “The God of my father was my helper and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.” (Exodus 18:4) Eliezer, the second son, carries that reason in his name. Try carrying a testimony around every time somebody calls you for dinner.

This one is true, friend, and the text says it plainly. Moses named his other son Eliezer, and said, “The God of my father was my helper and delivered me from the sword of Pharaoh.” (Exodus 18:4) So the reason on the card matches the verse. It's an easy one to doubt because the sentence is so big.

explanations.answer: He bows down and kisses him
explanations.explanation: Moses went out to meet his father-in-law, bowed down and kissed him. (Exodus 18:7) Moses, Israel's leader, didn't send a message back or wait to be visited. He walked out himself, and I love that. Then the two of them went into the tent together.

explanations.answer: He sends the elders to meet him
explanations.explanation: Moses doesn't send anybody in his place. The text says Moses himself went out to meet his father-in-law Jethro. (Exodus 18:7) The elders show up later, when Aaron comes with them to eat bread with Jethro (Exodus 18:12). Moses did this welcome in person.

explanations.answer: He waits for him in the tent
explanations.explanation: The tent comes after the greeting, not before it. Moses went out to meet Jethro, bowed down and kissed him. Then they greeted each other and went into the tent. (Exodus 18:7) Moses wasn't sitting inside with his arms crossed, friend.

The text says the opposite. Moses told Jethro all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, and he also told him all the hardships they had encountered along the way. (Exodus 18:8) Then he told how the LORD had delivered them. He gave Jethro the whole picture, rough patches and all.

Right, he didn't skip a thing. Moses recounted what the LORD did to Pharaoh and the Egyptians, all the hardships they had met along the way, and how the LORD had delivered them. (Exodus 18:8) Hardships and deliverance both made the telling. A story with only the highlights is like a cookie box with no cookies, friend.

The text says Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel. (Exodus 18:9) He is Moses' father-in-law, and he was happy for them. When good news is true, it can fill a whole tent.

The verse doesn't say fear. It says Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel, whom He had rescued from the hand of the Egyptians. (Exodus 18:9) Good news about a rescue is a reason to celebrate. Jethro was celebrating.

Doubt isn't in this verse. Jethro rejoiced over all the good things the LORD had done for Israel. (Exodus 18:9) And a few verses later he says, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods…” (Exodus 18:11). That sounds like a man who is sure, friend.

Jethro says, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods…” (Exodus 18:11) Notice the words “Now I know.” He heard the whole account first, and then he said it. I think that's how you want somebody to reach a conclusion, friend.
Jethro never says older. He says the LORD is greater than all other gods. (Exodus 18:11) His point is about who the LORD is, not about how long He has been around. Greater is the word the verse uses.

Gentler isn't what Jethro says here. He says, “Now I know that the LORD is greater than all other gods…” (Exodus 18:11) He's talking about the LORD being greater, and the reason he gives is what the LORD did when Egypt treated Israel with arrogance. It's a statement about the LORD's greatness.

Jethro brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. (Exodus 18:12) He had just blessed the LORD with his words, and then he brought something with his hands too. Words first, then an offering, and he did both in front of God.

explanations.answer: A tithe of his flocks and herds
explanations.explanation: No tithe shows up in this verse. The text says Jethro brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. (Exodus 18:12) That's the offering the verse names. I won't add flocks and herds to it, friend, because the text doesn't.

explanations.answer: A gift of gold and silver
explanations.explanation: The verse doesn't mention gold or silver. What Jethro brought was a burnt offering and sacrifices to God. (Exodus 18:12) That's all the text tells us he brought. Stick with what the verse says, friend.

explanations.answer: Why Moses sits alone as judge
explanations.explanation: Jethro asked, “Why do you sit alone as judge, with all the people standing around you from morning till evening?” (Exodus 18:14) He saw everything Moses was doing and asked about it. It's a fair question, friend. I would've asked it too, and I would've brought a chair.

explanations.answer: Why Moses keeps changing his rulings
explanations.explanation: Nobody says anything about changing rulings. Jethro asked what Moses was doing for the people, and why he sat alone as judge with everyone standing around him from morning till evening. (Exodus 18:14) His question was about the one man doing all the work.

explanations.answer: Why Moses won't hear the elders
explanations.explanation: Elders aren't part of Jethro's question. He asked, “What is this that you are doing for the people? Why do you sit alone as judge…?” (Exodus 18:14) The trouble he saw was Moses sitting there by himself while the people stood around him all day.

That's what Moses says. He replies, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God.” (Exodus 18:15) So the people weren't just lining up for a ruling. They came to Moses to ask about God. It's a weighty job, friend.
This one is true. Moses answered Jethro, “Because the people come to me to inquire of God.” (Exodus 18:15) The card says the same thing in different words. The text backs it up.

Jethro says, “…the task is too heavy for you. You cannot handle it alone.” (Exodus 18:18) Heavy is the word he picked. I think anybody who's ever carried too many boxes up the stairs knows what he means, friend.
Jethro doesn't say unclear. He says the task is too heavy for Moses. (Exodus 18:18) The problem is how much there is to carry, and carrying it alone. Nothing in the verse says the job was confusing.

Costly isn't the word in the verse. Jethro says that Moses and the people with him will wear themselves out, “because the task is too heavy for you.” (Exodus 18:18) He's talking about weight, not price. The load was too big for one man.

Jethro says the opposite. He tells Moses, “Teach them the statutes and laws, and show them the way to live and the work they must do.” (Exodus 18:20) Moses keeps that job. What Jethro wants shared out is the judging of the smaller cases, not the teaching.

Right, Jethro doesn't hand the teaching off. He says to Moses, “Teach them the statutes and laws, and show them the way to live and the work they must do.” (Exodus 18:20) That part stays with Moses. The sharing comes later in the plan.

Jethro says, “…select capable men from among the people—God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain.” (Exodus 18:21) Capable is the first word. Then he names two more things, God-fearing and trustworthy. The list was about character, friend.

Money and family names aren't on Jethro's list. He says to select capable men from among the people, God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain. (Exodus 18:21) The list is about who they are, not what they own.

Battle isn't in this verse. Jethro asks for capable men from among the people, “God-fearing, trustworthy men who are averse to dishonest gain.” (Exodus 18:21) These leaders were chosen for what kind of men they were. Nothing in the verse mentions fighting.
Jethro describes them as men “who are averse to dishonest gain.” (Exodus 18:21) That means they want no part of it. Think of it as a leader who counts crumbs honestly, friend.

Strong drink isn't on Jethro's list. He says these men are to be “averse to dishonest gain.” (Exodus 18:21) That's the thing they must want nothing to do with. The verse names that one, so that's the one I'll go with.

Idle talk doesn't appear in this verse. Jethro says the leaders should be God-fearing, trustworthy men “who are averse to dishonest gain.” (Exodus 18:21) That last part is what the card is asking about. It's the only thing the verse says they must stay away from.

Jethro says, “Then they can bring you any major issue, but all minor cases they can judge on their own…” (Exodus 18:22) The big ones go up to Moses. The small ones stay with the new leaders. That gives Moses room to breathe, friend.

If every case still came to Moses, nothing would change. Jethro's plan is that the leaders bring Moses any major issue, but all minor cases they can judge on their own. (Exodus 18:22) The little ones stop at the leaders, so the load gets lighter.

Jethro never limits it to cases between leaders. He says they can bring Moses “any major issue,” and judge all minor cases on their own. (Exodus 18:22) The dividing line is how big the case is. Who is arguing doesn't come into it.

Jethro says, “If you follow this advice and God so directs you, then you will be able to endure, and all these people can go home in peace.” (Exodus 18:23) Endure is the word he uses. Moses had been wearing himself out, so I think that word means a lot. The people get to go home in peace too.

Teach is in the plan, but it isn't the word in this verse. Jethro says Moses will be able to endure, and all these people can go home in peace. (Exodus 18:23) Earlier he told Moses to teach them the statutes and laws (Exodus 18:20). Here the promise is that Moses can endure.

Travel isn't what Jethro promises. He says, “…then you will be able to endure, and all these people can go home in peace.” (Exodus 18:23) The word is endure. This plan is about carrying the load without wearing out.

The text says Moses chose capable men from all Israel. (Exodus 18:25) It doesn't say he drew them from one tribe, friend. He made them heads over the people as leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.

Right, it wasn't just one tribe. Moses chose capable men from all Israel and made them heads over the people. (Exodus 18:25) They became leaders of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens. He looked across the whole people to find them.

The text says, “Then Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own land.” (Exodus 18:27) Jethro came, saw, gave his advice and headed home. He packed a lot into one visit, friend. I've never made a visit that useful.

This one is true. Moses sent his father-in-law on his way, and Jethro returned to his own land. (Exodus 18:27) The visit ended and Jethro went home. The new leaders kept judging the people while he was away.
